concepts.name: The components of a generative AI platform
RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context

questions.prompt: Chip Huyen builds her generative AI platform up from a bare call to a model. Which component does she add first?

choices.text: Context construction, such as retrieval (RAG) and query rewriting
A model gateway, so every team shares one API and its keys are kept safe
A semantic cache, to cut cost and latency on repeated queries
Write actions, so the model can change external systems on the user's behalf

questions.explanation: Her steps are: enhance context, put in guardrails, add a model router and gateway, reduce latency with caches, then add complex logic and write actions, with observability and orchestration across all of them. Context comes first because it improves answers most directly. Write actions come last because they carry the most risk.

questions.prompt: Sketch Chip Huyen's generative AI platform from memory: list its components in the order she adds them and say what each one does.

model_answer.summary: Start from a model call, then add context, guardrails, a router and gateway, caching, and complex logic with write actions, with observability and orchestration running across the whole system.
key_points: Context construction: retrieval (RAG), query rewriting and tools that fetch the information the model needs
Guardrails on the input (such as masking private data before an external API) and on the output (such as checking format and quality)
A model router that classifies intent to pick a model or pipeline, and a gateway that gives one secure, unified way to reach models
Caches to reduce latency and cost, then complex logic (loops) and write actions that change external systems
Observability (logs, metrics, traces) and orchestration that chains the components together

questions.explanation: Being able to draw this from memory is a common system-design interview test. Knowing the order also tells you why: each step adds capability and risk, so the riskiest pieces, such as write actions, come last.

questions.prompt: In Chip Huyen's platform, what does the model router do?

choices.text: It balances load between replicas of the same model to keep latency low
It stores provider API keys, tracks spend and enforces each team's budget
It retries failed calls on another provider whenever the first provider errors out
It predicts the user's intent and picks a fitting model or pipeline for the query

questions.explanation: The router uses an intent classifier to predict what the user wants, then sends the query to the right solution, such as a cheaper model for simple queries or a canned answer for out-of-scope ones. Keys, spend tracking, load balancing and fallbacks are gateway jobs.

questions.prompt: Why is a semantic cache riskier than an exact cache?

choices.text: It adds an embedding call, so it's slower than calling the model
It hits on similar embeddings, so a merely similar question can get a wrong answer
It can only store short answers, so long ones get cut off
It stops the provider's prompt caching from working on every request that it misses

questions.explanation: An exact cache only hits on an identical query. A semantic cache hits on a similar one, and depends on the embedding, the vector search and a similarity threshold, each of which can be wrong. Chip Huyen calls its value more dubious for this reason, and Eugene Yan notes that some practitioners see it as a disaster waiting to happen.

questions.prompt: Which workload benefits most from a plain exact-match cache?

choices.text: An open-ended chat where every conversation is different
An agent whose answers depend on live tool data
A summary generated for each product page, keyed by product ID and version
A creative-writing feature that samples at high temperature

questions.explanation: The applied-llms authors call caching underrated and suggest keying it on a unique ID for the item being processed, such as a product or article. The same input comes back often and the right answer doesn't change until the item does. Open chats rarely repeat, live data goes stale, and creative output is meant to vary.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an input guardrail?

choices.text: Masking personal data in a query before it's sent to an external model
Checking that the model's answer is valid JSON before the app parses it
Scoring the answer for toxicity before showing it to the user
Retrying when the model returns an empty answer

questions.explanation: Input guardrails act before the model sees the query: preventing private data leaking to external APIs, and blocking bad prompts such as jailbreaks. Checking format, toxicity or empty answers happens after generation, so those are output guardrails.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between input and output guardrails, with an example of each, and say what the system should do when an output guardrail fails.

model_answer.summary: Input guardrails check or change what goes into the model; output guardrails check what comes out. A failed output check triggers a recovery step, not a crash.
key_points: Input guardrails run before the model: for example masking personal data before an external API call, or blocking a jailbreak prompt
Output guardrails run on the answer: for example checking format (valid JSON), quality, toxicity or leaked sensitive data
When an output check fails: retry, or generate more than one answer in parallel and pick the better one
Escalate to a human for high-risk or ambiguous cases

questions.explanation: Chip Huyen treats failure management as part of the guardrail. Detecting a bad answer only helps if the system knows what to do next.

questions.prompt: Why does applied-llms recommend RAG over fine-tuning for adding new knowledge?

choices.text: Fine-tuning can't change a model's behaviour or knowledge at all
RAG always gives lower latency than a fine-tuned model, since no training is involved
Fine-tuned models can't use retrieved documents in their prompts once they are trained
Indexes update cheaply, bad documents can be dropped at once, and access checked per user

questions.explanation: The authors point to research where RAG beats fine-tuning for new knowledge, and to practical wins: updating an index is cheap, a problematic document can be deleted quickly, and retrieval can respect per-user permissions. Fine-tuning is better for teaching a task or a style, not for facts that change.

questions.prompt: A teammate says that million-token context windows make retrieval unnecessary: just put every document in the prompt. What do the applied-llms authors argue?

choices.text: They agree: long context replaces RAG for any corpus that fits in the window
Keep retrieval: all-in prompts cost more, run slower, and irrelevant text hurts reasoning
Long context only works reliably with fine-tuned models, so fine-tune first
Retrieval is only needed for keyword search; long context already covers semantic search

questions.explanation: Their heading is that long-context models won't make RAG obsolete. You still have to pick what's relevant: sending everything multiplies cost and latency, and more irrelevant context makes the model's reasoning worse. They also recommend keeping keyword search as a baseline and in hybrid search.

questions.prompt: Which practice makes LLM-as-judge evaluations more reliable, according to applied-llms?

choices.text: Ask for a score from 1 to 10 with no reasoning, so the judge can't ramble
Always put your own system's answer first so the judge reads it with full attention
Compare answers pairwise, swap their order to control position bias, and allow ties
Prefer the longer answer when the judge is unsure, since it's usually more complete

questions.explanation: Their tips: use pairwise comparisons instead of absolute scores, swap the order of the two answers because judges prefer one position, allow ties, ask for reasoning before the verdict, and control for length because judges favour longer answers. They also warn that LLM-as-judge works only somewhat and is no silver bullet.

questions.prompt: Why do the applied-llms authors recommend pinning model versions?

choices.text: A provider update behind an unpinned alias can silently change your app's behaviour
Pinned versions are always cheaper per token than the latest alias
Providers delete unpinned models every month, so unpinned apps break without notice
Pinning is required before a model will accept structured-output schemas

questions.explanation: Moving prompts between models is painful, and a new version can shift results noticeably. Pin a specific version in production, and run the newer one in a parallel shadow pipeline with your evals before you switch.

questions.prompt: Your team uses an unpinned model alias. The provider updates it, and answer quality drops for a week before anyone notices. Using applied-llms' operational advice, what would you change?

model_answer.summary: Pin the model version and trial upgrades against evals in a shadow pipeline, and look at real inputs and outputs every day so drift shows up in days, not weeks.
key_points: Pin a specific model version in production instead of an alias that can change
Run a new version in a shadow pipeline with your evals before switching production to it
Look at samples of production inputs and outputs every day, so a quality change is noticed quickly
Watch for differences between development and production data (dev-prod skew), and turn failures into eval cases

questions.explanation: Most of applied-llms' operational advice is about noticing change early: in the model, in the data, and in what users send.
